To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relationship between dental-related potentially hospitalisations and access to non-hopital dental services is complex and that the association between dental-related hospitalisations and access varies by the type of hospitalisation (potentially preventable vs. potentially avoidable).
Dental-related potentially preventable admissions to hospital and emergency department presentations are not indicators of poor access (financial and/or geographic) to dental care.
In summary, our research is concerned with
hospital admissions and ED presentations for dental-related potentially preventables, and not with the accessibility to non-hospital oral health care in the general population.
the association of dental-related potentially avoidable hospitalisations (PAHs) with socioeconomic disadvantage.
the accessibility of dental services in Western Australia, particularly the accessibility of non-hospital services.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to suggest that the high rates of potentially preventable hospitalisation and ED presentations for dental problems are due to lack of access to dental care.
the association between accessibility (both geographic and financial) to a non-hospital dental service and potentially preventable dental hospitalisations is unclear.
there is no evidence of poor access to dental services in Western Australia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between accessibility to non-hospital and hospital dental services and dental-related potentially preventible hospitalisations is not as simple as it seems.
dental-related potentially preventables hospitalisations were not associated with poor access to non-dental health services.
dental-related potentially preventably hospitalisations are associated with socioeconomic advantage and greater access to non-hosptial dental services, rather than poor accessibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dental-related potentially preventables are not an indicator of poor access to dental services in the community.
dental-related potentially preventables hospitalisation rates were not associated with access to dental services.

high rates of dental related potentially preventable hospital admissions in Western Australia are not due to poor access to dentists, but rather due to poor oral health and access to hospital services.
